## 1. Introduction

The purpose of this analysis was to examine how sampling distributions would behave when applied to 5 different populations. In order to achieve this, I used the Monte Carlo simulation with 10,000 repetitions for a sample size of 5, 10, 20, 30, 50, 100, and 200. In order to do so, I generated independent samples from Standard Normal, Six-Sided Die, Exponential, Binomial Small, and Cauchy populations. For each sample size, I calculated the sample mean, standard deviation, theoretical standard error, as well as histograms, normal Q-Q plots, skewness, kurtosis, and numerical summaries. 

## 2. Results

**Standard Normal Distribution**

1.  Results

    ```{r}
    #| echo: false
    #| warning: false
    #| message: false
    #| fig-show: hide

    code_lines <- readLines("Project1.R")

    end_line <- grep(
      "FINAL COMPARISON TABLE",
      code_lines,
      fixed = TRUE
    )[1]

    eval(parse(text = code_lines[1:(end_line - 1)]))

    knitr::kable(normal_summary, digits = 4)
    ```

2.  Interpretation

    Since the means are very close to 0, it shows it is very close to normal. The theoretical standard errors and simulated standard deviations are also very similar. The skewness is very close to 0, indicating that the sampling distribution is mostly symmetrical. Finally the kurtosis is very close to 3, which means it is close to a normal distribution.

3.  Histogram

    ```{r}
    hist(normal_results[["5"]],
         main = "Standard Normal Sampling Distribution, n = 5", 
         xlab = "Sample Mean")
    ```

    ```{r}
    hist(normal_results[["30"]],
         main = "Standard Normal Sampling Distribution, n = 30", 
         xlab = "Sample Mean")
    ```

    ```{r}
    hist(normal_results[["100"]],
         main = "Standard Normal Sampling Distribution, n = 100", 
         xlab = "Sample Mean")
    ```

    All of the histograms display a bell shape, which means they are normal.

4.  Q-Q Plot

    ```{r}
    qqnorm(
      normal_results[["5"]],
      main = "Q-Q Plot: Standard Normal, n = 5"
    )

    qqline(normal_results[["5"]])
    ```

    ```{r}
    qqnorm(
      normal_results[["30"]],
      main = "Q-Q Plot: Standard Normal, n = 30"
    )

    qqline(normal_results[["30"]])
    ```

    ```{r}
    qqnorm(
      normal_results[["100"]],
      main = "Q-Q Plot: Standard Normal, n = 100"
    )

    qqline(normal_results[["100"]])
    ```

    The lines all follow a straight line for all sample sizes which means it is normal.

5.  Conclusion

    Since the original population is already normally distributed, the sampling distribution will be normal for every sample size, and not just when it equals 30.

4.  Q-Q Plot

    ```{r}
    qqnorm(
      die_results[["100"]],
      main = "Q-Q Plot: Six-Sided Die, n = 100"
    )

    qqline(die_results[["100"]])
    ```

    The lines follow a straight line for all sample sizes, which means that it is normal.

5.  Conclusion

    The results seem to become more and more normal as the sample size increases and suggest that n=30 is enough for a sampling distribution to be approximately normal.

**Exponential**


2.  Interpretation

The simulated standard deviations decrease as the sample size increases, however they stay similar to the theoretical standard errors. The skewness below shows a right skew, but as sample size increases, it becomes more normal. The kurtosis also moves closer to 3 as the sample size increases.

3.  Histogram

    ```{r}

         main = "Exponential Sampling Distribution, n = 5", 
         xlab = "Sample Mean")
    ```

    ```{r}

         xlab = "Sample Mean")
    ```

    ```{r}
    hist(exponential_results[["100"]],
         main = "Exponential Sampling Distribution, n = 100", 
         xlab = "Sample Mean")
    ```

    There is a slight right skew for all histograms, meaning they are not normal.

4.  Q-Q Plot

    ```{r}
    qqnorm(
      exponential_results[["5"]],
      main = "Q-Q Plot: Exponential, n = 5"
    )

    qqline(exponential_results[["5"]])
    ```

    ```{r}
    qqnorm(
      exponential_results[["30"]],
      main = "Q-Q Plot: Exponential, n = 30"
    )

    qqline(exponential_results[["30"]])
    ```

    ```{r}
    qqnorm(
      exponential_results[["100"]],
      main = "Q-Q Plot: Exponential, n = 100"
    )

    qqline(exponential_results[["100"]])
    ```

    The Q-Q plot does not follow a straight line for any of the sample sizes, meaning it is not normal.

5.  Conclusion

    Considering the results of the table, the histogram, and Q-Q plot, it can be inferred that n=30 is not enough for an exponential distribution. The best possible sample size for exponential is n=100;

## 3. Is n=30 Enough?

The simulations suggests that n=30 is accurate for some, but not for all populations.

The **Standard Normal** population would benefit from **n=5**. This sampling distribution is already normal, meaning that any sample size, including the smallest, is sufficient for this population.

The **Six-Sided Die** population would find sufficient results with a **n=30**. The mean, standard error, skewness, and kurtosis, all result in normality. The graphs and plots also result in a normal distribution.

The **Exponential** population would most benefit from **n=100**. The histograms for n=5 and n=30 both showed a large right skew. The Q-Q plot do not follow a straight line, but becomes more and more straight as the sample size increases. This suggests that a larger sample size is more sufficient.

The **Binomial Small** population would benefit from **n=30**. The n=5 histogram showed a slight skew, but by n=30, it evened out into a normal bell shape. The skewness is very close to 0, and the kurtosis is close to 3.

The **Cauchy** population would **not benefit from any sample size**. This is because it does not ever converge into a normal sample size based on the table summary results, the histograms, and the Q-Q plots.

## 4. Limitations

**Limited Sample Size**

The results are based on a finite number of simulations, meaning that the results could be more accurate with larger sample sizes. This simulation does not identify the exact sample size that would display when each population becomes normal.

**Defining Normality**

Since many of these population distributions do not have a general indicator of when it is approximately normal, it is hard to find accurate results. The results of the summary, histograms, and Q-Q plots will not always have consistent conclusions.

**Specific Population Distributions**

This experiment only follows the results of five population distributions: Standard Normal, Six-Sided Die, Exponential, Binomial Small, and Cauchy. Since it does not include other population distributions, it is unknown if their results will have different levels of skewness or variance. This means that the conclusions found in this experiment cannot be generalized to every population distribution.

## 5. Conclusion

The results demonstrate that the Central Limit Theorem does not apply to every sampling distribution. However, even after finding a sample size that works for each of the distributions, that also does not imply that it is perfect and works for other sampling distributions. This simulation shows why numerical evidence and graph analysis is most important when evaluating different distributions and normality.
